title: Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA)
summary: RCRA is the foundational federal statute governing solid and hazardous waste and is the legal spine of U.S. materials recovery. Its stated objectives include resource conservation and recovery and reducing waste generation. Section 6002 directs federal agencies to buy products containing recovered materials (the buy-recycled mandate implemented via EPA's Comprehensive Procurement Guidelines), creating guaranteed government demand for recycled feedstock. It also authorizes EPA's solid-waste planning, guidelines, and grant authorities that later programs (e.g., SWIFR) build on.

title: Pollution Prevention Act of 1990
summary: The Pollution Prevention Act established a national policy that pollution should be prevented or reduced at the source, and where not feasible, recycled in an environmentally safe manner, explicitly placing source reduction and recycling above treatment and disposal in the waste hierarchy. It created EPA's source-reduction office, a Source Reduction Clearinghouse, matching state grants, and Toxic Release Inventory source-reduction/recycling reporting. This entrenched the reduce-reuse-recycle hierarchy that underpins circular-economy policy and drives industrial materials-efficiency data collection.

title: Mercury-Containing and Rechargeable Battery Management Act
summary: Known as the Battery Act, this statute phased out mercury in batteries and created a national, uniform framework for the collection, recycling, and proper disposal of rechargeable (Ni-Cd and small sealed lead-acid) batteries. It mandated easy-to-remove/labeled rechargeable batteries and preempted the patchwork of state rules to enable a nationwide takeback and recycling system (the model later run by Call2Recycle). It is the earliest federal producer-responsibility-style takeback mandate for a consumer product stream.

title: Marine Debris Research, Prevention, and Reduction Act
summary: This Act created NOAA's Marine Debris Program as the standing federal authority to identify, assess, prevent, reduce, and remove marine debris, including plastic waste that escapes the materials-management system. It funds research, removal grants, and interagency coordination and is the statute later reauthorized and expanded by the Save Our Seas Acts. It functions as an enabler by targeting plastic leakage at the end-of-pipe and building the data and grant infrastructure for prevention.

title: Microbead-Free Waters Act of 2015
summary: This Act amended the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to prohibit the manufacture and interstate distribution of rinse-off cosmetics containing intentionally added plastic microbeads. It is a federal design-out-of-plastic-pollution mandate: rather than manage the waste, it eliminates a non-recoverable microplastic at the product-design stage. Included as a narrow but clear federal enabler on the source-reduction/plastics axis.

title: Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007
summary: EISA drives resource efficiency across the federal enterprise and the economy, including federal building/fleet efficiency, a renewable fuel standard, and Section 525 sustainability and recovered/biobased procurement obligations for agencies. Its circular-economy relevance is chiefly materials- and energy-efficiency and federal green-procurement mandates rather than a recycling takeback scheme.

title: Save Our Seas Act of 2018
summary: The Save Our Seas Act reauthorized and amended NOAA's Marine Debris Program through 2022 and promoted international action to reduce marine debris, including plastic waste. It strengthened federal authority to respond to severe marine-debris events and engage source countries. It is the bridge statute between the 2006 Marine Debris Act and the far broader Save Our Seas 2.0 Act.

title: Save Our Seas 2.0 Act
summary: Save Our Seas 2.0 is the most comprehensive federal marine-plastics and recycling-infrastructure statute, organized around three pillars: strengthening U.S. domestic capacity (a Marine Debris Foundation, a Genius Prize, and a federal strategy), improving waste and recycling infrastructure, and international engagement. Section 302 authorized the grant authorities EPA now runs as the Solid Waste Infrastructure for Recycling (SWIFR) and Recycling Education and Outreach programs, and it mandated studies on recycling markets, standardization, and a federal microplastics/mismanaged-waste strategy. It is the statutory backbone of the current federal recycling-infrastructure push.

title: Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (Bipartisan Infrastructure Law)
summary: The IIJA delivered the largest-ever federal appropriation for recycling and materials-recovery infrastructure, funding the grant programs authorized under Save Our Seas 2.0: roughly $275M for Solid Waste Infrastructure for Recycling (SWIFR) grants and $75M for Recycling Education and Outreach grants, plus battery-supply-chain funding under Section 40207. It converts prior authorizations into actual money for collection, sortation, and end-market development. Sub-programs with distinct authorities are cataloged separately; this entry is the parent statute.

title: Agriculture Improvement Act of 2018 (2018 Farm Bill)
summary: The 2018 Farm Bill reauthorized and amended the biobased-markets provisions at 7 U.S.C. 8102 that govern the USDA BioPreferred Program, sustaining the mandatory federal preference and the voluntary USDA Certified Biobased Product label. By keeping renewable, biobased materials in the mandatory procurement stream, it supports the biological-cycle side of the circular economy (renewable feedstocks substituting for fossil-based inputs). Listed as the reauthorizing statute; the operating program is the BioPreferred entry.

title: Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Part 23 - Environment, Sustainable Acquisition
summary: FAR Part 23 makes sustainable acquisition binding on federal contracting officers, requiring that a high percentage of new contract actions deliver products that are, among other attributes, made with recovered materials, biobased, or otherwise environmentally preferable. Subpart 23.4 operationalizes recovered-material and biobased-product procurement (tying to EPA's CPG and USDA's BioPreferred designations) into solicitations and contracts. It is the demand-side lever that turns statutory buy-recycled/buy-biobased mandates into enforceable purchasing rules across roughly $600B/yr of federal spend.

title: EPA Comprehensive Procurement Guideline (CPG) for Products Containing Recovered Materials
summary: The CPG is EPA's regulation implementing RCRA Section 6002: it designates categories of products (paper, construction materials, park/recreation, landscaping, transportation, vehicular, and non-paper office products) that federal and federally funded procuring agencies must buy with recovered/recycled content to the maximum extent practicable, once annual purchases exceed $10,000. Paired with EPA's Recovered Materials Advisory Notices setting recommended recycled-content ranges, it guarantees pull-through demand for recycled commodities. It is the core federal recycled-content procurement mandate.

title: Executive Order 14057 - Catalyzing Clean Energy Industries and Jobs Through Federal Sustainability
summary: EO 14057 set government-wide sustainability goals directing agencies to use their purchasing power for sustainable products and services, including recycled-content, biobased, and low-embodied-carbon (Buy Clean) materials, and to advance waste diversion and a circular economy in federal operations. It reinforced the CPG/BioPreferred mandates and added embodied-carbon materials procurement. It was in force from December 2021 until it was rescinded by Executive Order 14148 ('Initial Rescissions of Harmful Executive Orders and Actions') on January 20, 2025 — a marker of the federal circular-procurement rollback, retained here for the historical record.

title: Executive Order 13834 - Efficient Federal Operations
summary: EO 13834 directed federal agencies to meet statutory sustainability requirements in an efficient, cost-effective manner, including reducing waste and diverting materials and continuing recovered-material and sustainable acquisition obligations. It was superseded by EO 14057 on December 8, 2021, so it is retained for historical/provenance completeness rather than as current in-force policy.

title: USDA BioPreferred Program
summary: The USDA BioPreferred Program, authorized by Section 9002 of the 2002 Farm Bill (7 U.S.C. 8102) and reauthorized in later Farm Bills, runs two circular-economy levers: a mandatory federal purchasing preference for USDA-designated biobased product categories (~139 categories, each with a minimum biobased-content threshold) above a $10,000 threshold, and a voluntary USDA Certified Biobased Product consumer label. It shifts federal and contractor demand from fossil-based to renewable, biologically cycled feedstocks.

title: EPA National Recycling Strategy / U.S. National Recycling Goal
summary: Released November 15, 2021, the National Recycling Strategy is EPA's federal roadmap (Part One of a broader circular-economy series) to build a more resilient municipal recycling system, organized around five objectives: improve markets for recycled commodities, increase collection/infrastructure, reduce contamination, enhance policies, and standardize measurement/data. It operationalizes the U.S. National Recycling Goal to reach a 50% recycling rate by 2030. It is guidance/strategy rather than a statute, so no legal full text exists.

title: Solid Waste Infrastructure for Recycling (SWIFR) Grant Program
summary: SWIFR is EPA's competitive grant program (authorized by Section 302 of Save Our Seas 2.0 and funded by the IIJA) that awards money to states, territories, tribes, and local governments to improve post-consumer materials management, expand collection and recycling/composting infrastructure, and develop end-markets for recycled materials, tracked against the National Recycling Goal. It is the primary federal capital pipeline turning recycling-infrastructure authority into deployed collection and processing capacity.

title: Consumer Recycling Education and Outreach (REO) Grant Program
summary: The REO grant program, funded with $75M through the IIJA (implementing the Save Our Seas 2.0 / RECYCLE Act authority), makes grants to improve the effectiveness of residential and community recycling and composting through public education and outreach, including a national recycling toolkit and campaigns to reduce contamination and wasted food. It attacks the behavioral bottleneck (contamination and low participation) that limits recycling-system yield.

title: DOE Battery Materials Processing and Battery Manufacturing and Recycling Grant Program
summary: Authorized by Section 40207 of the IIJA and administered by DOE (MESC/NETL), this multi-billion-dollar grant program funds domestic battery-materials processing, manufacturing, and end-of-life recycling and second-life reuse to close the loop on critical minerals and reduce reliance on virgin extraction. It is the federal industrial-policy lever building U.S. battery circularity across the upstream-to-recycling supply chain.
